chapter_theme: Paripadal 1 and 2, to Thirumal: the god in the fused forms of Balarama and Krishna, his ornaments and his war on the Danavas, his unknowability and identity with all things, the ages of the world in the order of the elements, the boar, the rank of the two brothers left open, the sacrifice as his food, and prayers to dwell at his feet with kin and to keep a mind without crookedness.

paripadal:1:1-13.reading: The song opens on two forms of Thirumal: first the one with the thousand awful hooded heads spitting fire rising over his crown, a body white as a flawless conch, the plough with its curved mouth and a single earring; then the one with eyes like clustered fire-flowers, a body like the opened kaaya bloom, Tiru seated on his chest among bright jewels and a golden garment like fire running over a great hill, lord of the male-bird banner, whom the eloquent brahmins' rare scripture tells of.
paripadal:1:1-13.nuance: The first five lines carry Balarama's emblems (the serpent hood, the conch-white body, the plough, the one earring) and the next five Krishna's (dark kaaya colour, Tiru on the chest, the golden garment), yet all are addressed to one god in the second person singular (ஒருவனை, கண்ணை, மேனியை): the poem fuses the two brothers into a single object of praise. The thing raised on the tall staff in line 4 (வேழம்) is not secure: elephant or reed; the known banner of the plough-bearer is the palmyra.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his forms and emblems: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:1:14-28.reading: In a dense run of compounds the poet piles up the god's ornaments: worked golden flowers, gems from the wilds strung with pearls, a garland on a famed chest bright as sunlight, a fire-pointed weapon, and the arrow that won the war against the Danavas who rose roaring to fight the gods until their heads poured blood like a stream.
paripadal:1:14-28.nuance: Lines 14 to 28 are written for sound more than syntax, in short chiming words (இணைபிரி அணி துணி பணி எரி புரை; நெறி செறி வெறி உறு முறல் விறல்), a sung, metrical display that suits a song set to music; the grammar of the run can be guessed but not fixed, and the reading above gives only its gist. The sentence closes on the single word கணை, the arrow, at line 28.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's ornaments and his victory over the Danavas, praise under paadaan

paripadal:1:29-39.reading: Hailing the faultless lord who broke the pride of those who said 'we will fight', the father of two, Maal with shining jewels, the poet says that even sages of clear inquiry can hardly know his coming, so how could it be easy for us to say he is such and such; knowing how hard it is, yet driven by longing, he asks the god with Tiru's mark on his chest not to scorn as weak the words we speak here, but to grant grace.
paripadal:1:29-39.nuance: The ineffability is argued a fortiori: if sages free of confusion (மருள் அறு தேர்ச்சி முனைவர்) cannot know him, singers cannot; the hymn then asks pardon for itself, so that the praise in the following lines is offered as acknowledged inadequacy. Who the two are whose father he is (இருவர் தாதை) is not said in the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: an address to the god asking grace, praise under paadaan

paripadal:1:40-51.reading: The poet tells the god what he is: the aram that the great brahmins guard and the tenderness shown to those who love him, the valour that set right the faithless and the terror of his foes, the moon shining in the lovely sky and the burning sun, the mighty one of the five upraised heads and the lion, the sense-field of flawless vision with the flower and its scent, the rising cloud, the vast sky, the earth and the tall Himalaya.
paripadal:1:40-51.nuance: Every line ends on நீ (you): this is identity, not likeness, and no comparison marker appears. The pairs are built as a king's praise is built (grace to friends and terror to foes, moon and sun), but cosmic items follow the moral ones, so that aram and the Himalaya are predicated of the god in the same breath. ஐந் தலை and மடங்கல் are not secure: the five-headed one may be the serpent or a god, and மடங்கல் may be the lion or the fire of the world's end.

thinai_evidence.note: the god praised as all things: paadaan

paripadal:1:52-68.reading: Therefore, since we see no one here of whom to say 'you are like these, you are such', and since he is the first of all lasting lives who holds the gold-adorned discus, the god is like only himself; his forms have fame like his, garments like gold, the bird banner, the twisted conch, the discus that killed the scornful, bodies like a washed gem and fame past counting; and so, the poet says, we, of joyful and secure heart, with our dear kin, pray to dwell together at your feet and prosper every day, worshipping the shade of your feet, poet of the true word.
paripadal:1:52-68.nuance: The hymn ends its search for a likeness by comparing the god to himself (நின்னோர் அனையை, நின் ஒக்கும் புகழ்): a poetics built on comparison turns the device on its own subject and finds no vehicle. The attributes of lines 58 to 63 are in the plural (நிழலவை, உடையவை, கொடியவை), as if of his many forms. The god is finally named a poet (வாய்மொழிப் புலவ), the author of the true word, the singers' own calling raised to him. The prayer asks for life together with kin (சுற்றமொடு), not for release.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing prayer of a hymn: paadaan

paripadal:2:1-19.reading: The poet tells the ages of the world in order: when the golden world and the earth went to waste and age upon age passed in the sky, came the age of the formless one that appeared as sound in the sky where the embryo grew, the age of the driving wind, the age of blazing red fire, the age of dew and cold rain, and within them, after flooding and filling and gathering again, the age of the great earth; past the counts named by numbers, the god made known one age, named for the boar's form, so that no one knows ages enough for his age, and the poet worships him, lord of the discus.
paripadal:2:1-19.nuance: The ages follow the order of the elements: sky (as sound), wind, fire, water, earth, each born of the one before, a cosmogony told as history. நெய்தல், குவளை, ஆம்பல், சங்கம், கமலம், வெள்ளம் in lines 13 and 14 are not flowers here but the names of vast numbers, the counts by which ages are reckoned; they are therefore left out of karu. Line 2 is broken in the text, so the opening clause is incomplete.

thinai_evidence.note: the god praised as older than the ages: paadaan

paripadal:2:20-35.reading: To those who say he is younger than the pure white one like a conch, the god is younger, and to those who call him elder to the lord of the palmyra banner with the dark garment, he appears elder; he is the centre of the flawless scripture studied by men of spotless rule, and whoever inquires into this finds his ancient greatness in his present state; his stainless chest, where the red goddess dwells like the spot on the moon amid ornaments curved like the rainbow and pearl garlands, is praised, and so is the deed of the white-tusked one who wedded the earth amid the waves, so that no word of those who think on it can mark it.
paripadal:2:20-35.nuance: Both halves of lines 20 to 23 name the same brother, Balarama (white like conch; the palmyra banner), so the poet does not decide between the traditions that make Thirumal his younger or his elder: the god takes the rank the worshipper gives him. In line 30 the chest is the moon and the goddess on it its dark mark, a figure that turns the Srivatsa mark into a moon spot. Lines 32 to 35, on the boar and the earth, are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's greatness and his chest praised: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the goddess on the god's chest

paripadal:2:36-51.reading: Those who rose together in fury, unbending, roaring against the thunder and swift as the wind, had their banners broken, their ears deafened, their crowns shaken and their footing lost, their loud conches and crowns destroyed, and their heads, garlands and all, rolled down, falling at once like countless clusters from tall dark palmyras torn up root and trunk, rolling, split, crushed and scattered, pouring mire till the earth sank: such is the weapon the god bears, which takes the lives of foes; his body is the Death that devours his enemies, and its colour is a flickering flame shining like gold.
paripadal:2:36-51.nuance: The long simile of the uprooted palmyras is built in the same breathless chain of verbal participles (ஒருங்கு உருண்டு, பிளந்து, நெரிந்து, உருள்பு சிதறுபு) as the fall of the enemies, so sound and sense fall together. The god's body is not likened to Death but called it (கூற்றம் உடலே), the strongest form of puram praise turned on a god.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's weapon and victory in battle, praise under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the god's body to his foes

paripadal:2:52-60.reading: The poet gives what the eloquent brahmins' rare scripture says of the god: his shining light is the dark sapphire, his eyes a pair of blooming lotuses, his truth the bright day, his patience the great earth, his grace the full sky; he is like that and the others, and he is also this and the one in every place, lord of the high banner of the red-beaked eagle.
paripadal:2:52-60.nuance: Lines 58 and 59 work with the Tamil pointing letters: அவ்வும் (that, the far), உவ்வும் (this, the near) and எவ்வயினோயும் (whichever place): the god is whatever any demonstrative can point to. Line 57 repeats Paripadal 1 line 13 word for word, a fixed refrain of the Thirumal songs.

words: நா வல் அந்தணர் அரு மறைப் பொருளே
thinai_evidence.note: the god praised as all things, paadaan

paripadal:2:61-76.reading: The teacher's words told in the scripture, the seizing of the goat in the sacrifice of the proper order, and the kindling of the fire by the chanted rite to take the abundance of its bright flame are food that comes with the god's own form, the coming that the brahmins see as equal to him, which others will not accept; to him who sealed the nectar in and went for the immortals, giving them unaging tradition and unceasing strength, the poet and his many kin bow their heads at his feet, praise and bless him with quiet hearts, and pray: may our understanding never know crookedness.
paripadal:2:61-76.nuance: The animal of the sacrifice (ஆடு) is counted among the god's food without hesitation; the hymn sides with the brahmins' rite against those who do not accept it (பிறர் உடம்படுவாரா), a hint that the rite already had dissenters. The closing prayer asks not for wealth or release but for a mind without crookedness (கொடும்பாடு). Line 72 is broken, so the deed of lines 69 to 72 cannot be fully construed.

thinai_evidence.note: the god as the recipient of the sacrifice, and the closing worship: paadaan

links.note: Purananuru 56.3-6 sets out the conch-white plough-bearer with the palmyra banner and the gem-dark one with the bird banner as two of four separate gods; Paripadal 1.3-11 gives the same emblems (வால் வளை மேனி, நாஞ்சில், சேவல் அம் கொடி) to one god addressed in the singular.
links.teaches: Held together, the pair shows that the emblem sets of Balarama and Thirumal were fixed common iconography, but that the Paripadal's Vaishnava singer had already fused the two brothers into one object of worship that the puram poet still counted as two gods.

links.note: Paripadal 1.32-33 says Thirumal's coming is hard to know even for sages free of confusion; Tirumanthiram 13 puts Vishnu who measured the earth among the gods who, measuring by thought, still cannot conceive the Lord. On the plain reading the two give the unknowable highest place to different gods, and one puts the other's god among the baffled seekers.
links.teaches: The same argument from unknowability served two rival theologies, and the Saiva poet reuses it by moving Thirumal from the place of the unknown into the place of the seeker, so ineffability became a way to rank gods.

links.note: Purananuru 59 tells the Pandya he is like the sun to his foes and like the moon to us (ஞாயிறு அனையை ... திங்கள் அனையை); Paripadal 1.41-45 tells the god he is grace to those who love him and terror to foes, the moon and the burning sun, with no marker of likeness.
links.teaches: The devotional poet took the king-praise formula of grace to friends and fire to foes and dropped its marker of comparison, so what the court poet offers as a simile becomes in the hymn a statement of identity.

links.note: Purananuru 56 makes the Pandya equal (ஒத்தீயே) to each of four gods in one quality; Paripadal 1.53-57 says no one can be found of whom to say the god is like them, so he is like only himself (நின்னோர் அனையை); both describe the bird-bannered god's body with the same formula, மண்ணுறு மணி (Pura 56.5, Pari 1.62).
links.teaches: The pairing shows a limit to the பூவைநிலை way of praising a king by the gods: the likeness runs one way only, since a king can be measured by a god but the hymn finds nothing by which to measure the god.

links.note: Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without comparison (தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான்) are freed from the mind's care; Paripadal 1.53-68 finds no likeness for the god (நின்னோர் அனையை) and ends with hearts made secure (ஏமுறு நெஞ்சத்தேம்) worshipping the shade of his feet.
links.teaches: The couplet's two terms, the incomparable one and refuge at his feet, appear in the hymn as a sequence: the singer first tries and fails to find a simile, and only then turns to the feet, so the Kural's maxim reads as the summary of a hymn's movement.

links.note: Paripadal 2.5-12 tells the ages of the world in the order sky (as sound), wind, fire, water, earth; Thiruppugazh 21 names Mayon as the one who became sky, wind, fire, water and earth in the same order, and the seven worlds, yet touches none of them.
links.teaches: The five-element order credited to Thirumal survives a thousand years into Arunagirinathar, but what the Sangam singer told as successive ages of the world's making the later poet states as the god's present pervasion of all things.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 7 declares the Lord elder to the three (மூவர்க்கும் மூத்தவன்) and father to the one who calls him father; Paripadal 2.20-23 makes Thirumal younger to those who call him younger than the conch-white brother and elder to those who call him elder.
links.teaches: Both poets let the god become the kin-name the worshipper uses, but only the Paripadal applies the rule to seniority itself, so where Tirumular fixes his Lord as eldest the earlier hymn shows rank among gods as a matter of the believer's tradition.

links.note: Paripadal 1.1-5 addresses Thirumal with Balarama's emblems as one god (ஒரு குழை ஒருவனை); Paripadal 2.20-23 names the conch-white palmyra-banner brother as a second figure and leaves open whether Thirumal is his younger or his elder.
links.teaches: Read together, the two hymns show that the fusion of the brothers in the first song was a devotional claim made against a known two-brother story, which the second song keeps in view by refusing to settle their order.

links.note: Kural 1 takes the letter அ, first of all letters, as the figure of the First Lord who is first of the world; Paripadal 2.58-59 uses the pointing letters அ, உ and எ (அவ்வும், உவ்வும், எவ்வயினோயும்) to say the god is that, this and whatever place.
links.teaches: Two early poets built theology from the Tamil alphabet in different ways: the Kural uses the order of the letters to make God the origin, while the hymn uses the pointing letters to make God every possible referent, origin set beside pervasion.

links.note: Paripadal 2.62-65 counts the seizing of the goat in the sacrifice and the fire oblation as the god's own food; Kural 259 says not to take one creature's life and eat it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices. On the plain reading the hymn honours the animal sacrifice that the couplet ranks below abstention.
links.teaches: The hymn's aside that others will not accept the brahmins' rite (பிறர் உடம்படுவாரா) and the Kural's ranking of not killing over sacrifice show the same quarrel from both sides, so the dispute over animal sacrifice was live within the Tamil tradition itself.

new_concepts.gloss: a cosmic age: one of the long periods of the world's making and unmaking, counted in succession
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's word (Paripadal 2, lines 4 to 18: ஊழி ஊழ்ஊழ் செல்ல ... ஊழி யாவரும் உணரா)

source_issues: Paripadal 1: the colophon names no poet, composer or pan (flag); the subject is திருமால்.
Paripadal 1 line 17: மணியொடும் has its vowel sign restored by rule (யடு/ளடு to யொடு/ளொடு); sangamtamil.com does not confirm it here (flag).

Paripadal 1 lines 20-21: நவையினிற் / றுணி divides one word across the line break, and line 16 (திரடெரி) and line 25 (வயிறிரிய) are printed with sandhi unsplit; the dense run of lines 14 to 28 is hard to segment.
Paripadal 1 line 13 and Paripadal 2 line 57 are the same line (flag): a refrain of the Thirumal songs, not a copying error.
Paripadal 2 lines 2 and 72 have gaps in the source (lacunae); the opening clause and the deed of lines 69 to 72 cannot be fully construed.
Paripadal 2 lines 52 and 61: flagged for a dropped heading line; read by eye, the text runs on without a visible gap at both points (51 to 52 and 60 to 61).

Paripadal 2 line 1 differs strongly from sangamtamil.com's text and lines 19, 20, 29, 37 and 40 are not in it; ours kept (flags). Lines 7 and 8 were repaired and line 35 has a vowel sign restored by rule (flags).
Paripadal 2: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan பாலையாழ் is a musical mode, not a thinai.
